rule: The Commissioner must investigate and attempt to settle any industrial dispute that exists or may arise.
The Commissioner may refer any industrial dispute for conciliation, arbitration, or to a labour tribunal.
A collective agreement in force is binding on all parties and its terms are part of their employment contracts.
The Commissioner or authorized officer must attempt to settle any dispute referred for conciliation.
A settlement must be in writing and signed by both parties or their representatives.
Any valid settlement is binding on all parties and becomes part of their employment contracts.
Employees have the legal right to challenge termination by applying to a labour tribunal.
Contract clauses cannot override worker rights granted by labour tribunals.
Complaints about termination must be filed within six months.
Retrenchment protections apply only to employers with 15 or more employees.
Employers must give written notice before retrenching an employee.
Retrenchment cannot occur until two months after notice is given.
Employers cannot force union membership or non-membership.
Employees cannot be dismissed for union involvement.
Employers must negotiate with unions that represent at least 40% of workers.
Labour tribunals can order reinstatement of dismissed workers.
Employers may be ordered to pay compensation for wrongful dismissal.
Employers cannot punish workers for participating in legal proceedings.
Employees cannot be punished for claiming lawful employment benefits.
Any contract clause that limits worker rights under this Act is invalid.
Retrenched workers must be given priority when rehiring.
An employee must not be employed for more than 8 hours per day or 45 hours per week (excluding rest/meal breaks).
If an employee has worked earlier for another employer that day, the total hours for both employments must not exceed the legal daily limit.
An employee must be given one full holiday and one half-holiday each week with pay if they have worked at least 28 hours that week.
In the first year of employment, an employee must be granted paid annual leave based on the start date (14/10/7/4 days).
From the second year onward, an employee is entitled to at least 14 days of paid annual leave, including at least 7 consecutive days.
Annual leave must be taken in the year after the year of employment with dates agreed by employer and employee.
An employee is entitled to up to 7 days of paid casual/medical leave per year.
In the first year, casual leave accrues at 1 day per 2 months of service.
From the second year onward, casual leave may be taken during that year.
Approved absences do not affect service continuity.
On termination, the employee must be allowed unused annual leave with pay or be paid in lieu if leave cannot be taken.
Employees retain leave rights during notice periods
An employee must be given paid public holidays, up to 9 days per year.
If an employee works on a public holiday, they must receive a replacement holiday or double pay.
An employee must be granted a holiday on each Full Moon Poya Day.
If an employee works on a Full Moon Poya Day, they must be paid at least 1.5× the normal daily rate.
An employee must be given meal intervals as specified in the Act’s Schedule.
No person under 16 years old may be employed in a shop or office.

Employees aged 16–18 (male) and all female employees cannot be employed before 6 a.m. or after 6 p.m., except: (i) females 18+ in hotels/restaurants until 10 p.m., (ii) females 18+ in residential hotels, (iii) females 18+ in shops/offices until 8 p.m., (iv) males 16+ in hotels/restaurants/entertainment until 10 p.m., (v) females 18+ in IT/BPO/back offices

act: Shop and Office Employees Act, No. 19 of 1954
rule: Employers must provide adequate lighting and ventilation.

act: Shop and Office Employees Act, No. 19 of 1954
rule: Employers must provide sanitary and washing facilities, including separate female facilities.

act: Termination of Employment of Workmen Act
rule: An employer must not terminate a worker’s employment unless the worker gives written consent or the Labour Commissioner gives prior written approval.

act: Termination of Employment of Workmen Act
rule: The employer must give the worker a copy of the termination request and allow the worker to respond before a decision is made.

act: Termination of Employment of Workmen Act
rule: The Labour Commissioner has full authority to approve or reject a termination request.

act: Termination of Employment of Workmen Act
rule: The Commissioner must grant or refuse approval to terminate employment within 3 months of the employer’s application.

act: Termination of Employment of Workmen Act
rule: The Commissioner must notify both employer and worker in writing of the decision on a termination application.

act: Termination of Employment of Workmen Act
rule: The Commissioner may set terms and conditions for termination, including gratuity or compensation payable by the employer.

act: Termination of Employment of Workmen Act
rule: The Commissioner’s decision on termination approval cannot be challenged in court.

act: Termination of Employment of Workmen Act
rule: The worker must be informed within 3 days and given 7 days to respond to a termination request.

act: Termination of Employment of Workmen Act
rule: Disobeying the Commissioner’s order is a criminal offence.

act: Termination of Employment of Workmen Act
rule: Employers must pay a daily fine for continuing to ignore the Commissioner’s order.

act: Termination of Employment of Workmen Act
rule: Termination includes any form of non-employment by the employer, whether temporary or permanent, including termination due to business closure, but excluding disciplinary dismissal.

act: Termination of Employment of Workmen Act
rule: Employers must give written reasons within 2 working days for disciplinary termination.

act: Termination of Employment of Workmen Act
rule: The Act applies only to employers with 15 or more workers.

act: Termination of Employment of Workmen Act
rule: A worker is not protected by this Act if their total period of employment is less than 180 days, even after counting approved leave, injury leave, occupational disease leave, employer-caused work stoppages, lawful strikes or lockouts (up to 30 days), and statutory holidays.

act: Termination of Employment of Workmen Act
rule: Retirement-related termination is excluded from this Act.

act: Termination of Employment of Workmen Act
rule: Workers covered by this Act are excluded from Industrial Disputes Act retrenchment rules.

act: Termination of Employment of Workmen Act
rule: A termination that violates this Act is illegal and has no legal effect.

act: Termination of Employment of Workmen Act
rule: If a termination is unlawful, the Commissioner may order reinstatement and payment of wages and benefits, and the employer must comply.

act: Termination of Employment of Workmen Act
rule: If employment is terminated due to business closure in violation of the Act, the Commissioner may order compensation instead of reinstatement.

act: Termination of Employment of Workmen Act
rule: Workers must complain within 6 months of termination.

act: Termination of Employment of Workmen Act
rule: Compensation amounts are calculated according to a Gazette formula determined by the Commissioner and Minister.
An employer must not employ a woman worker during the four weeks immediately after her confinement.
A woman worker is entitled to 12 weeks of maternity benefit for a live child: 2 weeks before confinement + 10 weeks after.
A woman worker is entitled to 6 weeks of maternity benefit for a still birth: 2 weeks before + 4 weeks after.
If a woman worker worked any days during the 2‑week pre‑confinement period, she is entitled to maternity benefit for the same number of days after the standard period ends.
If the woman worker dies during her maternity benefit period, she (or her nominee) is paid benefits only up to the day of her death.
An employer must pay maternity benefit at the prescribed rate for the full statutory period (12 weeks for live birth, 6 weeks for non‑live), including extra days under the proviso rule.
Maternity benefit periods are in addition to any other leave or holiday rights the woman worker has.
A woman worker may give notice to her employer of her expected confinement within one month before the date.
After confinement, a woman worker must give notice within one week of the confinement date and indicate if it was a live birth.
A woman worker may nominate someone to receive her maternity benefit on her behalf.
An employer must allow the woman worker to be absent for the full statutory maternity benefit period.
If the woman worker dies, the employer must pay due maternity benefit to her nominee or her legal heir.
An employer must not dismiss a woman worker during maternity absence, nor have notice expire during that absence.
An employer must not terminate employment solely because of the worker’s pregnancy, confinement, or related illness.
If a worker gives notice of expected confinement, the employer must not assign her work harmful to her or her child during pregnancy and 3 months after confinement.
After confinement, the employer must not employ the worker in harmful work for 3 months.
If there is a dispute about whether a dismissal notice given to a woman worker was for sufficient cause, the matter must be decided by the Commissioner of Labour, whose decision is final.

A woman worker who is nursing a child under one year of age must be allowed two nursing intervals within any nine-hour work period. Each interval must be at least 30 minutes if a creche or suitable place is provided, or at least one hour if not provided, and these intervals are in addition to other breaks and count as paid working time.
If the employer has more than the prescribed number of women workers, it must provide and maintain a crèche for children under five and allow eligible workers to use it.
Employers must pay gratuity to workmen who have completed the minimum service period.
If the employer dies, the legal representative is responsible for paying the gratuity.
The rate of gratuity depends on the employee’s role and period of service.
The Commissioner certifies the gratuity amount owed by an employer.
Gratuity must be paid when an employee with sufficient service is terminated.
Late gratuity payments incur additional surcharges.
Gratuity is calculated based on wage or salary for each year of service.
Employees who are domestic servants or entitled to a non-contributory pension are not eligible for gratuity.
The Employer may withhold or forfeit gratuity if termination is due to proven misconduct causing loss.
Gratuity must be paid to heirs if the employee dies before receiving it.
Gratuity for employees in converted public companies can be paid via cash or bonds.
Bonds issued as gratuity accrue interest and can be encashed under specified conditions.
The Commissioner can inspect employer records for gratuity compliance.
Employers must comply with official directions to provide records for gratuity verification.
Service under previous employers counts toward gratuity if ownership changes within five years.
Employees must contribute 8% of their monthly earnings to the Employees’ Provident Fund for each month worked in covered employment.
Employers must pay 12% of the employee’s monthly earnings to EPF by the last day of the following month.
EPF contributions can be voluntarily increased above statutory minimums.
If an employer reduces an employee’s earnings to lower EPF contributions, the Commissioner can direct the employer to pay the difference.
Employers must pay a surcharge for late contributions ranging from 5% to 50% depending on the period of delay.
All contributions and interest must be credited to the employee’s individual EPF account.
Employers must not reduce an employee’s earnings or benefits because of EPF obligations.
Employers cannot deduct EPF contributions or surcharge from employee wages; contracts attempting this are void.
EPF funds cannot be assigned or attached except as permitted by law.
The Employees’ Trust Fund Board must be set up to administer and manage the Fund.
The Board must maintain a general Fund account and individual accounts for each member.
Employers must contribute 3% of each employee’s monthly earnings to the Fund, payable by the last day of the following month.
All ETF contributions must be credited to the employee’s individual account.
If an employer makes higher voluntary contributions, 3% must go to ETF, and any excess may be allocated to approved provident funds.
Self-employed persons or migrant workers may join the Fund voluntarily by notifying the Board in writing.
ETF contributions earn statutory interest, at a minimum rate of 3% per annum, as fixed by the Board
On termination of employment, the employee is entitled to receive the amount standing to their credit in the Fund, subject to statutory conditions.
Withdrawals from individual ETF accounts are restricted to once every 5 years, except for members over 60 or those permanently leaving Sri Lanka.
Rights to the Fund’s monies are strictly limited to statutory provisions; no additional or extrastatutory claims are allowed.

act: Employment of Women, Young Persons, and Children Act
rule: Persons under 18 cannot be employed at night in industrial undertakings.

act: Employment of Women, Young Persons, and Children Act
rule: Night work for women is allowed only voluntarily, with Labour Commissioner approval, additional pay, welfare supervision, rest facilities, and maximum 10 nights per month.

act: Employment of Women, Young Persons, and Children Act
rule: Young persons may not be employed at night except as permitted by law.

act: Employment of Women, Young Persons, and Children Act
rule: No child under 14 may be employed in industrial undertakings.

act: Employment of Women, Young Persons, and Children Act
rule: Employers must maintain accurate employment registers for women and young persons.

act: Employment of Women, Young Persons, and Children Act
rule: No person under 15 may be employed on Sri Lankan or Sri Lanka-connected vessels.

act: Employment of Women, Young Persons, and Children Act
rule: Employment details of children must be disclosed to authorized officers when requested.

act: Employment of Women, Young Persons, and Children Act
rule: Children cannot participate in entertainment for which payment is charged.

act: Employment of Women, Young Persons, and Children Act
rule: No person under 18 may be employed in hazardous occupations.

act: Employment of Women, Young Persons, and Children Act
rule: Employers and guardians must provide employment information of women and young persons to authorized officers when requested.

act: Employment of Women, Young Persons, and Children Act
rule: Labour officers may inspect workplaces and investigate compliance.

act: National Minimum Wage of Workers Act, No. 3 of 2016
rule: Employers must pay every worker at least LKR 10,000 per month or LKR 400 per day, regardless of industry or service.

act: National Minimum Wage of Workers Act, No. 3 of 2016
rule: No employer may pay less than the national minimum wage, even if other laws allow lower payments.

act: National Minimum Wage of Workers Act, No. 3 of 2016
rule: Existing employees must not have reduced wages or benefits after the Act starts.

act: National Minimum Wage of Workers Act, No. 3 of 2016
rule: Employers must keep a wage register showing employee names, job type, and wages.

act: National Minimum Wage of Workers Act, No. 3(2)
rule: Wage registers must be kept for 6 years.

act: National Minimum Wage of Workers Act, No. 3 of 2016
rule: Labour inspectors can check compliance, review registers, and demand wage info from employers.

act: National Minimum Wage of Workers Act, No. 3 of 2016
rule: If wages are unpaid, the Commissioner-General can order the employer to pay the defaulted amount.

act: National Minimum Wage of Workers Act, No. 3 of 2016
rule: Non-payment can lead to court action and fines imposed by a Magistrate.

act: National Minimum Wage of Workers Act, No. 3 of 2016
rule: Violating minimum wage rules can result in fines up to LKR 25,000 or 6 months imprisonment.

act: National Minimum Wage of Workers Act, No. 3 of 2016
rule: Definitions: Employer = person/company hiring workers; Worker = anyone under a contract; National minimum wage = salary or allowance meeting minimum wage.
A landlord must not charge rent higher than the authorized or receivable rent fixed under the Act.
Advance rent cannot exceed three months of the lawful rent.
Extra payments such as key money or premiums are illegal.
A tenant must obtain written consent before subletting.
Unauthorized subletting allows lawful eviction through court.
Even tenants subletting must not charge above authorized or proportionate rent.
Landlord must not charge above fixed proportionate rent for parts of premises.
A landlord cannot separately charge for furniture or fittings.
A landlord must not cut off essential services such as water, electricity, or sanitation.
Force or harassment to evict a tenant is strictly prohibited.
A landlord must not interfere with a tenant’s lawful occupation.
For rent arrears eviction, advance notice is mandatory (3 months first time, 2 months second, 1 month thereafter).
Eviction for landlord’s own use requires one year’s written notice.
New owners cannot evict existing tenants for personal use in most cases.
Tenants can recover or deduct excess rent paid.
Landlords must provide a written rent statement when requested.
Rent receipts are mandatory for all payments.
Any document affecting land, ownership, or mortgages falls under this law and may require registration.
An unregistered land document is legally weaker and loses priority to a later registered document.
Sale deeds, transfers, mortgages, land agreements, wills, and court orders must be registered to affect land rights.
Pending court cases affecting land are not enforceable against buyers unless officially registered.
Land documents must clearly describe the property (location, boundaries, size) to be valid for registration.
Documents missing required land details can be legally rejected and treated as non-compliant.
The parties to the document or anyone with a legal interest can submit it for registration.
Registration time determines legal priority between competing land documents.

act: Consumer Affairs Authority Act No. 9 of 2003
rule: Manufacturers and traders must comply with labelling, price marking, and packaging directions issued by the Authority.

act: Consumer Affairs Authority Act No. 9 of 2003
rule: Selling goods above the marked price is illegal.

act: Consumer Affairs Authority Act No. 9 of 2003
rule: Goods or services must conform to standards and warranties. Failure requires compensation, replacement, or refund.

act: Consumer Affairs Authority Act No. 9 of 2003
rule: Agreements can set maximum prices for goods.

act: Consumer Affairs Authority Act No. 9 of 2003
rule: Traders cannot refuse to sell goods they have in stock for trade purposes.

act: Consumer Affairs Authority Act No. 9 of 2003
rule: Traders cannot impose conditions requiring purchase of additional goods or services (no forced bundling).

act: Consumer Affairs Authority Act No. 9 of 2003
rule: Traders cannot hoard goods beyond normal trading requirements.

act: Consumer Affairs Authority Act No. 9 of 2003
rule: Price increases for essential goods/services require Authority approval.

act: Consumer Affairs Authority Act No. 9 of 2003
rule: Traders must display price lists conspicuously in their business premises.

act: Consumer Affairs Authority Act No. 9 of 2003
rule: Traders must issue receipts showing date, quantity, price, and transaction type.

act: Consumer Affairs Authority Act No. 9 of 2003
rule: Traders cannot engage in misleading or deceptive conduct.

act: Consumer Affairs Authority Act No. 9 of 2003
rule: False claims about quality, standard, grade, style, or model are illegal.

act: Consumer Affairs Authority Act No. 9 of 2003
rule: Falsely claiming goods are new is illegal.

act: Consumer Affairs Authority Act No. 9 of 2003
rule: False claims about product features, benefits, or endorsements are illegal.

act: Consumer Affairs Authority Act No. 9 of 2003
rule: False claims about discounts or price changes are illegal.

act: Consumer Affairs Authority Act No. 9 of 2003
rule: False claims about necessity of goods, services, or repairs are illegal.

act: Consumer Affairs Authority Act No. 9 of 2003
rule: False claims about warranties or guarantees are illegal.

act: Consumer Affairs Authority Act No. 9 of 2003
rule: All service contracts have an implied warranty of due care and skill.

act: Consumer Affairs Authority Act No. 9 of 2003
rule: Materials supplied with services must be fit for their intended purpose.

act: Consumer Affairs Authority Act No. 9 of 2003
rule: All goods and services must meet determined standards and specifications.

act: Consumer Affairs Authority Act No. 9 of 2003
rule: All goods must be reasonably fit for their intended purpose.

act: Consumer Affairs Authority Act No. 9 of 2003
rule: When consumers specify a purpose, there is an implied warranty goods/services will be fit for that stated purpose.

act: Unfair Contract Terms Act No. 26 of 1997
rule: Contract clauses excluding liability for death or personal injury from negligence must be ignored.

act: Unfair Contract Terms Act No. 26 of 1997
rule: Contract clauses excluding liability for other loss/damage from negligence must be reasonable.

act: Unfair Contract Terms Act No. 26 of 1997
rule: Awareness or agreement to a negligence exclusion clause does not mean acceptance of risk.

act: Unfair Contract Terms Act No. 26 of 1997
rule: Cannot perform substantially different obligations than agreed.

act: Unfair Contract Terms Act No. 26 of 1997
rule: Cannot avoid performance completely unless contract term is reasonable.

act: Unfair Contract Terms Act No. 26 of 1997
rule: Consumer cannot be required to indemnify another’s negligence or breach unless reasonable.

act: Unfair Contract Terms Act No. 26 of 1997
rule: Guarantees cannot exclude liability for defective goods in consumer use.

act: Unfair Contract Terms Act No. 26 of 1997
rule: Guarantees cannot exclude liability for manufacturer/distributor negligence.

act: Unfair Contract Terms Act No. 26 of 1997
rule: Cannot exclude consumer protections for quality, fitness for purpose, and sale by sample.

act: Unfair Contract Terms Act No. 26 of 1997
rule: Cannot exclude consumer protections in hire-purchase agreements.

act: Unfair Contract Terms Act No. 26 of 1997
rule: Cannot use another contract to bypass protections under this Act.

act: Unfair Contract Terms Act No. 26 of 1997
rule: Reasonableness test: term must be fair given circumstances at contract formation.

act: Unfair Contract Terms Act No. 26 of 1997
rule: Party claiming reasonableness must prove it.

act: Unfair Contract Terms Act No. 26 of 1997
rule: Cannot avoid liability by imposing burdensome conditions.

act: Unfair Contract Terms Act No. 26 of 1997
rule: Cannot restrict remedies or penalize someone for pursuing rights.

act: Unfair Contract Terms Act No. 26 of 1997
rule: Cannot restrict rules of evidence or procedure via contract.

act: Sale of Goods Ordinance, No. 11 of 1896
rule: A sale of goods contract involves transfer of ownership for money.

act: Sale of Goods Ordinance, No. 11 of 1896
rule: A sale of goods contract must be evidenced in writing or performance (acceptance or payment).

act: Sale of Goods Ordinance, No. 11 of 1896
rule: Seller must have the legal right to sell the goods.

act: Sale of Goods Ordinance, No. 11 of 1896
rule: Buyer has right to quiet possession of the goods.

act: Sale of Goods Ordinance, No. 11 of 1896
rule: Goods must be free from unknown liens/encumbrances.

act: Sale of Goods Ordinance, No. 11 of 1896
rule: Goods sold by description must match that description.

act: Sale of Goods Ordinance, No. 11 of 1896
rule: If buyer states a specific purpose, goods must be fit for that purpose.

act: Sale of Goods Ordinance, No. 11 of 1896
rule: Goods bought by description must be of merchantable quality.

act: Sale of Goods Ordinance, No. 11 of 1896
rule: Express contract terms cannot remove implied warranties unless they directly conflict.

act: Sale of Goods Ordinance, No. 11 of 1896
rule: Goods sold by sample must match the sample in quality.

act: Sale of Goods Ordinance, No. 11 of 1896
rule: Goods sold by sample must be free from hidden defects.

act: Sale of Goods Ordinance, No. 11 of 1896
rule: Seller must deliver goods and buyer must accept and pay as agreed.

act: Sale of Goods Ordinance, No. 11 of 1896
rule: Delivery and payment must occur at the same time unless agreed otherwise.
Cash price must be disclosed in writing before entering a hire-purchase agreement.
Hire-purchase agreements not complying with statutory form and disclosure requirements are unenforceable.
Hire-purchase agreements must clearly state price, instalments, deposit, and goods details.
Mandatory statutory notice must be prominently included in the agreement.
Hirer must have quiet possession of the goods.
Owner must have the legal right to sell the goods.
Goods must be free from undisclosed charges or encumbrances.
Goods must be of merchantable quality unless a lawful exception applies.
Goods must be fit for the purpose made known by the hirer.
Goods sold by sample must match the sample.
Goods sold by description must match the description.
Fitness-for-purpose exclusions are invalid unless clearly disclosed.
Excessive hire-purchase charges must be reduced to statutory limits.
Hirer has a right to early purchase with rebate.
Clauses restricting the hirer’s right to terminate are void.
Hirer is entitled to compensation on unfair repossession.
Owner must give proper notice before terminating for default.
Goods cannot be repossessed without court action after 75% payment.
Owner must provide agreement copies and payment information on request.
Unfair hire-purchase clauses listed in the Act are void.
A person must be registered to legally run a finance leasing business.
Only approved financial institutions can get a finance leasing registration.
A lessee has a right to peaceful possession of leased equipment; the lessor must protect it.
A lessee must care for and properly use the leased equipment.
If the equipment is not delivered on time or is defective, the lessee may reject and end the lease.
At the end of the lease, the lessee must return the equipment unless ownership was agreed.
If the lessee defaults, the lessor can demand full payment, end the lease, reclaim equipment, and seek damages.
Before enforcing default rights, the lessor must serve a written notice specifying the default and a timeline to fix it.
Employers must pay wages in cash/legal tender directly to employees and cannot make unauthorized deductions.
Employers must set a wage period and pay wages within the legal timeframe (3–10 days depending on period length).
When employment ends, the employer must pay all wages due within two working days.
Employers must keep accurate written wage records including wages paid, dates, hours worked, and deductions.
Wage records must be kept for at least four years and produced when requested.
Employers must give a holiday on Poya days and pay at least 1.5× normal wage if work is done on that day.
A Wages Board sets mandatory minimum wage and overtime rates for specific trades.
Employers must pay wages at least at the minimum rate fixed by the relevant Wages Board.
Violating wage provisions can result in fines up to Rs. 5,000 or imprisonment up to 6 months, or both
Loan agreements must comply with Board-set maximum interest rates and loan term limits.
Microfinance NGO loan agreements must comply with maximum interest rates and other terms set by the Registrar.
Savings agreements issued by microfinance NGOs must comply with maximum interest rate limits set by the Registrar.
Loan agreements must include consumer protection measures as required by Registrar-issued rules.
Only licensed or exempt entities can provide microfinance services; agreements from unlicensed lenders are illegal.
Pawnbroker loan contracts must not charge interest above the legally specified maximum rate.
Pawnbroker loan agreements must allow redemption of pledged goods within 12 months.
Pawn contracts must allow redemption on surrender of pawn ticket foil and proper signature.
Pawnbroker must give 14 days notice before selling a pledged item.
After sale of a pledged item, the pawnbroker must pay the debtor any surplus within one year if demanded.

act: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, No. 7 of 1840
rule: Contracts involving land or immovable property must be in writing, signed by all parties, and notarised, otherwise they are legally invalid.

act: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, No. 7 of 1840
rule: Land transaction documents must include the thumb impression of each party, affixed before a notary and witnesses.

act: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, No. 7 of 1840
rule: Agreements to guarantee or be responsible for another’s debt must be in writing and signed to be enforceable.

act: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, No. 7 of 1840
rule: Contracts to pledge movable property are invalid unless the property has been physically delivered to the pledgee.

act: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, No. 7 of 1840
rule: Partnership agreements with capital exceeding Rs. 1,000 must be in writing and signed by all partners to be valid.
Contracts or clauses formed electronically (e‑contracts) cannot be treated as invalid just because they are electronic.
When a law requires writing, an electronic record that can be accessed later is legally equivalent to written form.
If a contract must be kept in original form, an electronic record that reliably preserves integrity counts as original.
Electronic signatures (e‑signatures) are legally valid if they identify the signer and show intent to authenticate the contract.
A contract formed by offer and acceptance electronically is valid and enforceable even if entirely digital.
If a contract uses electronic records or e‑signatures, it cannot be denied legal effect just because it uses digital formats or e‑signatures.
An electronic contract is deemed received when it arrives at the recipient’s designated electronic address and can be retrieved, not when actually read.
If an input error occurs in an electronic contract and cannot be corrected immediately, the person may withdraw that portion of the contract if notified promptly.
Electronic documents and records are admissible as evidence in court proceedings.
Courts will presume electronic documents and e-signatures are genuine unless proven otherwise.
A person who lends money and receives profit-based interest or a share of profits does not automatically become a partner and is not liable as a partner.
An employee or agent paid through profit-sharing does not become a partner and has no partnership rights or liabilities.
A widow or child receiving profit payments after a partner’s death is not considered a partner and is not liable for business debts.
A person who sold a business and receives ongoing profit payments is not a partner and is not liable for the business’s debts.
If the business becomes bankrupt or insolvent, a lender with profit-based interest can only recover after all other creditors are fully paid.
If a loan’s total charges (interest, fees, penalties) are excessive and the transaction is harsh or unfair, the court can review the loan and reduce the amount owed to what is fair.
For loans up to Rs. 100, any interest rate above 20% per year is presumed unreasonable unless the lender proves otherwise.
For loans between Rs. 100 and Rs. 2,500, any interest rate above 18% per year is presumed unreasonable unless the lender proves otherwise.
For loans over Rs. 2,500, any interest rate above 15% per year is presumed unreasonable unless the lender proves it is reasonable.
The total interest charged on a loan can never exceed the original principal amount at any point in time.
A loan agreement is invalid if obtained through undue influence where one party dominates the other and gains an unfair advantage.
Money lenders must keep clear written records of all loan transactions showing amounts, payments, and charges in plain language.
If a money lender fails to keep proper loan records, they cannot legally enforce the loan in court.
Every promissory note must clearly state the amount borrowed, any advance deductions, and the annual interest rate.
A promissory note that does not clearly state loan details cannot be enforced in court.
It is a criminal offence for a lender to accept a promissory note with a false or blank amount.
Money lenders are not allowed to harass or intimidate borrowers by targeting their home or workplace.
It is illegal for a lender to persuade a borrower’s spouse or child to take a loan without written consent.
